title: What not to put on the site for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: What to leave off a recruiting firm site
excerpt: Cut the handshake and the industry cloud. Keep the kind of role you fill and a way to brief the search. A shorter site that tells the truth is the stronger one.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, a display of taste that can crowd out the role a hiring manager came to find.
caption: A wall of frames can look finished and still hide the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove from a recruiting site?
faqs.answer: Remove the handshake photograph, including well-lit pictures of your own partners. It reassures the firm and does not show the kind of role you fill. Replace it with the workplace or the scorecard, or use fewer pictures until you have a frame that carries the role.

faqs.question: What should remain after the cut?
faqs.answer: Keep the kind of role, the way a search is briefed, one proof with a decision, and a path to brief the search. Bios and fees can stay when they are specific. A vague page kept only so the menu looks full is worse than a missing page.

faqs.question: How long should the site be?
faqs.answer: Long enough to name the role, the refusal, and the brief. People have time to read only about a quarter of the words on a typical visit, so extra blocks are a bet most visitors will not take. Add a page when you have a new role family, not when the menu looks thin.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The most common recruiting firm website mistakes start with a handshake photograph and a list of every industry the partners have ever touched. Both reassure the team. Both confuse a hiring manager who has been burned before. Keep the kind of role you fill and a clear way to brief the search. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long one that performs taste.

Nielsen Norman Group's account of attention is the practical limit. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. On the visits they do make, they have time to read only about a quarter of the words, and the average visit lasts a little less than a minute. Every extra block is a bet that they will read past the role. Most will not. Google's helpful-content guidance asks a related question: after reading, has someone learned enough to take the next step, or do they need to search again. A long page that never names the role sends them back to search.

## Cut the handshake first

The handshake is the mistake the firm defends hardest, because it feels human. The buyer already believes the work is human. They have sat through a kickoff. They want to know if you fill a seat like theirs. A photograph of two people clasping hands does not say plant manager, clinic lead, or controller. It says meeting.

Remove it from the homepage, the about page, and the proof pages. Replace it with the workplace of the role, or with the artifact you use, such as a scorecard. If you have no such frame yet, use fewer pictures. Empty space is more honest than a costume. Do not crop the handshake into a detail of sleeves and call it art direction. The subject is still a handshake.

The same cut applies to the skyline, the lobby sculpture, and the stock meeting with laptops and smiles. They are handshakes in different clothes. If a picture could be swapped onto another firm's site without anyone noticing, it is not carrying your role.

## The other performances of taste

Walk the page and mark anything that could be claimed by the firm that disappointed this buyer.

A counter of placements with no definition of a placement or a year. A cloud of industries. A five-step process in which every step is a synonym for "we talk to people." A values list: integrity, excellence, partnership. A carousel of logos you cannot discuss. An autoplay film of the office. A blog that does not mention the roles you fill. A navigation item called Solutions.

None of these is evil. All of them spend the quarter of the page the visitor might read. The values list is the clearest example. It reassures the people who wrote it. It gives the buyer no way to predict week three of a search. A single refusal does that job. "We do not start outreach before the scorecard is signed." That sentence can stay. "We value excellence" cannot.

Google's people-first questions are a useful edit. Does the page give a complete enough account that the reader can act. Does it show first-hand experience, or only a category. A page written to look like a recruiting firm, rather than to help a hiring manager brief one kind of search, is search-engine-shaped even when nobody said the word SEO in the room. Write for the buyer who might come directly. The category words can appear once, in a place a stranger expects, and then get out of the way.

## What stays

Keep four things, and be suspicious of a fifth.

The kind of role, in the words a hiring manager uses on a requisition. The way a search is briefed, including what you refuse. One proof with a constraint and a decision, even if the client is unnamed. A path to brief the search, with a promise you can keep about what happens next.

Who does the work can stay if the bios name the role family and the verbs. Fees can stay if they show the shape. If either is vague, do not keep a vague version for the sake of having the page. A missing page is cleaner than a page that says "bespoke."

Candidate content can stay as a quiet link. It should not share the first screen with the brief. Two equal doors are a mistake that feels fair in a workshop and fails on a phone.

## How to cut without a fight

The fight is usually about loss, not about the buyer. A partner likes the film. A board member likes the handshake. A marketer likes the industry cloud because it makes the firm feel larger.

Make the cut in a meeting with the page on a phone, not in a deck. Cover the screen after ten seconds. Ask what role the firm fills. If the answer is "recruiting," the covered material was not the problem. The first screen was. Uncover the rest only after that answer is right. People defend lower sections when the hero has already failed.

Give each defended item a test. If we delete this, what true thing does the buyer lose. If the answer is "our personality," ask which sentence carried the personality. Keep the sentence. Lose the block. Personality that requires a carousel is not personality. It is anxiety.

Write the removals down. "No handshake. No industry cloud. No placement counter without a definition. No second button for candidates in the hero." Pin the list where the next freelance designer will see it. Otherwise the handshake returns in the next refresh, because it is the default in their portfolio.

## Length is a decision

A short site is not a small firm. It is a firm that chose. Three offers with boundaries. Two proofs with decisions. One fee shape. One brief. An about page that names the people on the search. That is a complete site for this buyer.

Add a page when you have a new role family you are willing to be hired for, with its own sentence and its own refusal. Do not add a page because the menu looks thin, or because a competitor has a resource center. Nielsen's quarter-of-the-words finding means the resource center will not be read by the person who is deciding whether to brief you. It might be read later, by someone who already trusts you. Later is not a reason to put it above the role.

If a paragraph repeats the hero in softer words, delete the paragraph. Repetition feels like emphasis inside the firm. On the page it feels like padding. The visitor who stayed past half a minute, the point at which Nielsen notes people may stay much longer, will notice the padding and discount the rest.

## The candidate site hiding in the same pages

A second mistake is writing half the site for candidates and half for the person who pays. Open roles in the hero. "Join our network" as a button. A culture page above the fee. Candidates matter, and they will arrive. They are not the buyer this page is for. A hiring manager who has been burned reads a candidate-heavy site as a firm that is collecting resumes, which is what the last search felt like from their side of the table.

Give candidates one quiet path: a text link, a single page, a way to send a background. Do not let that path set the photography, the headline, or the first button. If you need a separate experience for candidates later, build it when the hiring path is clear. Mixing them to "serve both audiences" produces a site that serves the workshop. Each audience leaves unsure whether the firm is for them.

Read the homepage out loud and mark every sentence addressed to a job seeker. Move those sentences. If the page collapses without them, the role sentence was never doing the work. Write it, then put the candidate lines back in their own corner.

## A removal pass

Print the site, or scroll it once on a phone, and mark with a pencil.

1. Any picture of a handshake, a skyline, or a generic meeting.
2. Any number you cannot define in one clause.
3. Any heading that is a department rather than a role or a decision.
4. Any sentence that could be pasted onto a competitor's site unchanged.
5. Any second action that competes with the brief.

Delete the marks. Do not replace them with something of equal length. The gap is the point. Then read the role sentence and the brief to someone who hires. If they can repeat both, the site is shorter and truer. If they cannot, you deleted the wrong thing. Put that sentence back, and delete a different block.

When the recruiting site tells the truth about the role, a different buyer still needs a different page. A small consultancy is often compared with the buyer doing the work themselves, which is not the same fear as a failed search. Read [what that homepage has to prove](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-small-consultancy) if that is the firm you are actually building.

When you want to see a first screen that names the work before it performs taste, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful examples are the ones that could not be about someone else.
